item.title: AWS Introduces Centralized Workforce Access to IAM Roles Across Accounts
item.description:
AWS recently introduced Account Access Manager to centrally assign workforce users and groups to existing IAM roles across an organization, preserving custom trust policies and ABAC configurations while improving individual identity attribution and auditability.

By Renato Losio

item.title: Azure AI Gateway Reaches General Availability as a Standalone Service
item.description:
Microsoft has made Azure AI Gateway generally available as a standalone Azure service for governing access to AI models and MCP tools across providers. A free tier covers 10,000 requests per gateway per month; paid billing starts January 1, 2027; and private networking remains in preview.

By Steef-Jan Wiggers

item.title: Meta Brings Code Review Auto-Approval More Mainstream with PyTorch GreenLight
item.description:
PyTorch now lets an AI reviewer approve pull requests from its own maintainers. GreenLight is an open-source take on RADAR, the system Meta uses to auto-land low-risk diffs after safety checks, a risk score and an LLM review. OpenAI, Anthropic and Sonar describe similar ways to automate approval while keeping humans on risky changes.

By Andrew Hoblitzell

item.title: Netflix Builds Quasar to Measure the Blast Radius of Library API Changes
item.description:
Netflix developed Quasar, an internal tool that combines semantic code indexing and API comparisons to identify downstream consumers affected by library changes. Using SCIP, Amazon S3, and Athena, it traces API references across repositories, helping maintainers assess migration impact and make informed release decisions. Netflix is also exploring agent-assisted consumer migrations.

By Leela Kumili

item.title: Why SAP’s second 10,000-job overhaul in two years matters to CIOs
item.description:
When SAP restructured roughly 10,000 roles in 2024, executives framed the move as a workforce transformation designed to prepare the company for cloud computing and AI. Two years later, SAP is reportedly considering eliminating another 10,000 positions, but this time the rationale appears different.

Rather than reshaping skills while maintaining headcount, analysts say the latest overhaul reflects a growing belief among technology companies that AI can permanently reduce labor needs, raising new questions for CIOs about vendor stability, support quality, and the economics of the AI era.

The layoffs are expected to impact several departments, including product and engineering, according to a Bloomberg article that reported on the new round of layoffs.

While the 2024 restructuring did not reduce the headcount and was shown as a reshuffle of skills to align with the company’s AI-first strategy, the new round of layoffs appears to be focused on cost reduction and is likely to shrink the company’s employee count by about 9%.

“SAP’s 2024 programme changed who worked there, and this one is about how many,” said Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Grehound Research.

When SAP announced a major restructuring in 2024 affecting roughly 10,000 positions, executives described it as a strategic shift toward cloud computing and AI. The company took a restructuring charge of about €3 billion and repositioned talent toward growth areas, including AI.

SAP did not directly comment on the Bloomberg story, saying it does not comment on speculation. A company spokesperson, however, said, “The business environment in which we operate is changing rapidly through AI, and we are continuously reviewing how our organization and workforce need to evolve to remain successful. As part of this ongoing transformation, roles and functions will naturally change over time. Beyond this, no decisions have been made regarding any further measures.”

Looking beyond the employee count

For CIOs, the key issue is not the scale of the cuts. It is why a company that already undertook a major restructuring just two years ago believes another overhaul may be necessary.

“AI can reduce manpower requirements in software development, testing, documentation, customer support, pre-sales, and implementation activities. But Tech CEOs were arguing that, because of Jevons Paradox, AI will create more demand for software. In reality, that has not happened yet. CEOs who were saying AI will create more tech jobs are doing layoffs,” said Pareekh Jain, CEO at Pareekh Consulting.

Yet, SAP’s move toward this second restructuring is hardly a surprise, according to analysts.

Gogia describes the move as part of a three-step change at SAP. “First came the slow tightening: Klein’s 2025 talk of one or two per cent a year, then the July 2026 memo focusing new hiring on ‘mainly core AI roles.’ Next came the substitution, which Klein described plainly when he said SAP is balancing token consumption against headcount. Last came the declaration, when Asam told investors the episode of rising headcount was over and spoke of five-digit numbers of employees to be touched.”

Read in sequence, the Bloomberg report is less a surprise than the third step arriving on schedule, with tokens now the fuel the engine prefers to salaries, Gogia added.

What happens next

SAP avoided using terms such as layoffs or job cuts in its 2024 restructuring plan, terming the changes voluntary programs and internal retraining measures. At the same time, the company has also been unusually vocal about its internal AI gains.

“The autonomous enterprise SAP launched in May 2026 needs data scientists, agent builders and people who understand business processes deeply enough to teach software to run them. Nothing in that roadmap requires a cut of at least 10,000,” Gogia said.

The CIOs who sat through the 2024 reshuffle have reason to feel uneasy, because the first round tested their patience and this one tests their support desk. SAP’s board should publish where the cuts land, function by function, before the January results, said Gogia. CIOs should ask SAP, in writing and before any 2027 renewal, which of their service commitments depend on teams named in the programme, and what SAP will measure to prove service holds.”

item.title: How Adesso defies the AI cost spiral
item.description:
With the switch to agent-based software development, token consumption at Adesso increased exponentially, forcing the company to rethink its approach.

According to a recent KPMG study, while many companies have implemented initial measures to manage AI spend, transparency regarding actual operating costs remains limited. Nearly a quarter of the surveyed executives acknowledge difficulties with usage-based AI costs, and 42% have only a partial overview of AI expenditures.

In addition, 33% face challenges understanding AI cost structures, including tokens, which makes predicting, controlling, and optimizing spend more difficult.

Adesso CTO Frank Dobelmann knows the problem all too well. Costs have risen drastically as a result of switching from Agile to agent-based software development, where ​​token consumption alone has increased a hundredfold in a year.

For Dobelmann, these are growing pains that inevitably arise with disruptions as the experimentation phase draws to a close, and ROI becomes the focus. But this didn’t deter the company from curbing AI costs with its centralized hub that’s already amassed 450 billion tokens from approximately 4,800 employees.

The starting point was spring 2025. In a two-day off-site meeting, the company withdrew from its day-to-day operations to assess developments surrounding AI. Reps from SAP, Microsoft, Salesforce, and other tech providers, as well as international experts and influencers, offered insights into the market. One realization ran through all the presentations. “No one could predict the future, but everyone agreed that AI would become bigger than any technological change of recent years,” says Dobelmann.

This led to the decision to build a dedicated AI Force. Day-to-day operations leave no room to support such a profound transformation, so experts from various areas of software development were brought together to focus exclusively on the transformation to an agent-driven company and to guide its development.

An agentic awakening

Initially, the focus was on how to effectively deploy and operate code assistants locally to keep costs under control. However, this phase was short-lived. In the fall of 2025, a new stage of development began with powerful agentic models like Claude Opus.

“That was a real milestone for us,” says Dobelmann. “Suddenly it became clear the possibilities went far beyond classic code assistants.”

To familiarize employees with the new tools early on, the company provided all developers with access to leading AI models. Each developer received a monthly testing budget of €50, which wasn’t charged to their own cost center or manager. The goal was not to consume as many tokens as possible, but gain experience and build skills.

Yet the transition to agent-based software development fundamentally changed the picture. While usage increased slowly at first, token consumption grew exponentially.

Fortunately, the company established a central AI hub early on, an LLM-based gateway through which all local and external models from various providers were accessed. This meant detailed data on the usage and costs of all AI applications, from the company-wide chatbot to AI functions within software development, ​​were available from the outset.

“The invoices won’t arrive any later as a result,” he says. “But this way we have complete transparency regarding how our costs develop. This transparency is crucial.”

New cost item, but higher benefit

Dobelmann doesn’t view the rising token costs as inherently negative. However, agent-based software development introduces a new type of cost that wasn’t previously considered in traditional project and customer contracts.

“In 2024, practically no one factored token costs into their contracts,” he says. “Now we have to explain to customers that while this new cost item does arise, the economic benefits are significantly greater.”

To this end, Adesso gradually converted existing software projects from classic Agile to agentic development. During the transition phase, two teams worked in parallel: one continued to develop using classic Agile methods, while the other relied entirely on agentic development. Both approaches were compared using defined KPIs.

Only when the results were confirmed was the complete switchover carried out. Initially, fixed token budgets were agreed upon with the customers, as actual consumption couldn’t be reliably predicted at the start.

In retrospect, this approach has proven successful, says Dobelmann. Productivity gains of up to 60% were achieved in individual projects. However, the projects didn’t become smaller or cheaper as a result, but delivered significantly more software in the same timeframe, thus generating considerably higher business value.

Agents need guardrails

With the increased use of autonomous agents, another issue has moved to the forefront: their control, and the discipline has already evolved significantly. While the focus was first primarily on prompt engineering, today it’s about so-called harness or loop engineering, controlling agents safely and with the broadest possible impact within clearly defined parameters. This includes sandboxing mechanisms, clearly defined execution environments, and the principle of restricting agents to a single task as narrowly as possible.

“Our agents receive exactly one assignment and then terminate their engagement,” Dobelmann says. “This prevents them from building context over an extended period or independently taking on tasks we never assigned them.”

Internally, this principle is called Ronin Yolo, an architectural approach in which specialized agents perform only a clearly defined task and then terminate themselves. This keeps them controllable, efficient, and secure.

Transparency instead of gut feel

To assess the economic viability of agentic development, Adesso relies on a comprehensive system of KPIs based on the AI Hub. Dobelmann says this data will be made available to relevant employees via Power BI in the future to create transparency regarding costs incurred in consulting and implementation projects, or using different models.

“Right now, we’re just building on our experience,” he says. While traditional Agile software development can draw on decades of experience, there are only a few years of reliable data available for agent-based development. To be able to calculate projects more reliably in the future, telemetry data from all projects will be systematically collected and analyzed.

Economic efficiency as new developer criterion

Another insight recently gained is that the most powerful AI model isn’t necessarily the most economical choice. Many developers initially preferred the most expensive frontier models like Claude Opus, but the company responded by redefining standard models and providing developers with clear recommendations for the appropriate model deployment.

This also aligns with the recommendations of the model manufacturers themselves, according to Dobelmann. Not every task requires the most powerful model. So Adesso runs open-source models on its own GPU cluster and expands it appropriately.

He thinks the conscious and economical management of token consumption is becoming a new core competency for software developers. “Previously, developers had to program good software cleanly,” he says. “Today, they also have to keep an eye on token consumption and associated costs.”

Local models as strategic hedging

While building its own AI infrastructure involves significant investment, for a software company like Adesso, this effort quickly pays off. At the same time, though, it’s more than just a matter of cost.

“Local open-source models increase technological sovereignty and reduce dependence on US frontier models,” Dobelmann says. And should access to individual models be restricted by regulatory or geopolitical developments, the company will remain operational.

While open-source models often lag up to nine months behind the latest commercial models, they’re already powerful enough for many use cases. And due to their significantly lower operating costs, they represent an economically attractive alternative. Since the AI Hub was built to be multi-tenant capable, customers can now access these local models without having to operate their own infrastructure.

Productivity measured at the project level

Adesso rejects the idea of ​​evaluating the productivity of individual developers based on their token consumption. Instead, the focus is on the professional development of employees. To this end, a dedicated training program for agent-based software development was developed.

Bootcamps, specific training for developers, architects, and consultants, as well as gamified elements, are designed to facilitate entry and increase acceptance. Not every employee works on an agent-based project, though, so it’s all the more important to build skills early on since virtually every software project will contain AI components in the future. So success isn’t measured at the level of individual developers, but on the results of entire projects.

New agent-based business models

Increased productivity is also changing pricing in project-based business. According to Dobelmann, traditional fixed-price projects will regain importance.

Agent-based development allows for a more precise calculation of the scope of work, and enables complete modernization projects to be offered economically, like in the transformation of mainframe applications. Adesso now combines its own migration methods with agent-based software development in this area, and can realize projects that weren’t previously feasible economically.

In addition to traditional fixed prices, he expects more value-based compensation models in the future. If software development becomes significantly faster, billing based on time and materials will become less relevant. Instead, service providers could be more heavily involved in the actual business value generated, like through bonus-malus systems or profit-sharing. Furthermore, there’ll be models where token costs are transparently itemized as a separate cost and passed on to the customer. Dobelmann doesn’t specify concrete cost savings for the economic benefits of his own AI infrastructure. Nevertheless, investments in the local GPU cluster are recouped through savings on paid frontier models.

item.title: Mozilla Partners with Mistral to Bring Open-Weight AI Models to Firefox Smart Window
item.description:
Mozilla has partnered with Mistral AI to offer Mistral Small 4, an open-weight model, in Firefox's Smart Window AI assistant, now in beta. It is recommended for users in France, the US and Canada. Users can choose among several models, and Mistral agreed to zero data retention. Beta feedback is mixed.

By Daniel Curtis
